tutorial_example_entry.lesson_title: Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output
tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Interpret a piecewise convolution result as the time-domain output behavior of an LTI system determined jointly by the input signal and impulse response.

sections.lesson_title: Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Introduction to Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output

image_slots.image_description: Create a compact black-and-white technical diagram of an LTI system. Show an input arrow labeled $x(t)$ entering a rectangular system block labeled $h(t)$, and an output arrow labeled $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$. Beneath the block diagram, show three small aligned time axes labeled input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and output $y(t)$, with simple finite-duration sketches on each axis. Keep all labels readable and do not add numeric signal data.

blocks.text: For an LTI system, the impulse response $h(t)$ characterizes the system. When the input is $x(t)$, the output is the convolution of $x(t)$ with $h(t)$.

The convolution formula still tells you where $y(t)$ comes from, but in this lesson the main move is interpretation. Once the convolution has already been computed, treat the resulting piecewise function as the time-domain output signal $y(t)$.

For a finite-duration input and a finite-duration impulse response, the computed output is often a piecewise signal. A simple case has zero output before the signals overlap, a nonzero region where the output rises, reaches a peak or plateau, and then falls, and zero output again after overlap ends.

To interpret the result, first name the piecewise function as $y(t)$. Then read where $y(t)$ is zero, where it is nonzero, which breakpoints divide the time axis, and how the output changes on each interval.

Those breakpoints come from changes in overlap between $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$. Here, you use that overlap idea to explain the output behavior, not to recompute the convolution integral from scratch.

sections.lesson_title: Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Identifying the Convolution Result as the Output $y(t)$

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system has input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and the convolution has already been computed as (x*h)$(t)=g(t)$. Identify the system output $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the output rule is that the output equals the convolution of the input with the impulse response.
Here, the convolution has already been computed and named $g(t)$. Match the given statement to the output rule.
Since $y(t)$ is the convolution result, the system output is $g(t)$.
The output is not $x(t)$ alone, $h(t)$ alone, or the product $x(t)$$h(t)$. It is the computed convolution of the input and impulse response.

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white time-domain plot of the convolution output $y(t)$. Show a horizontal t-axis and a vertical $y(t)$-axis. Plot $y(t)=0 for t<a$, a nonzero finite-duration curve from $t=a to t=b$, and $y(t)=0 for t>b$. Label the breakpoints a and b on the t-axis, label the nonzero region $a<t<b$, and make the zero line visible before a and after b. Use no numeric values.

example_content.example_prompt: A plotted convolution output $y(t)$ is zero before $t=a$, nonzero from $t=a$ to $t=b$, and zero after $t=b$. Identify the zero and nonzero output regions.

explanation_blocks.text: The plotted curve is the computed convolution output, so read it as $y(t)$. The task is not to recompute the convolution integral; it is to read where the output exists over time.
Before the first breakpoint a, the graph lies on the zero line. Therefore the output is zero for times before a.
From a to b, the graph leaves the zero line. That interval is the nonzero output region.
After the second breakpoint b, the graph returns to the zero line. Therefore the output is zero for times after b.
So the output is nonzero from a to b, and it is zero before a and after b. The endpoint convention is not the main issue here; a and b are the support boundaries of the output.

sections.lesson_title: Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Connecting Piecewise Breakpoints to Changing Overlap

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with four aligned panels. Panel 1: a fixed rectangular support for $x(\tau)$ on a $\tau$-axis, labeled from its left endpoint to its right endpoint. Panels 2-4: matching $\tau$-axes showing the shifted support of $h(t-\tau)$ at $t=a$, $t=b$, and $t=c$, with overlap against $x(\tau)$ highlighted. At $t=a$, the right endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the left endpoint of $x(\tau)$. At $t=b$, the supports are aligned with maximum overlap. At $t=c$, the left endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the right endpoint of $x(\tau)$. Add a small $y(t)$ plot at the bottom with breakpoints a, b, and c marked, showing zero before a, a nonzero region split at b, and zero after c.

example_content.example_prompt: A finite-duration input and impulse response produce a piecewise output $y(t)$ with breakpoints at $t=a$, $t=b$, and $t=c$. Explain what changes in the overlap between $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ at each breakpoint.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that $y(t)$ is piecewise. A breakpoint in $y(t)$ marks a time when the overlap relationship between $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ changes. We will read the breakpoints in increasing order.
At $t=a$, the shifted support of $h(t-\tau)$ first touches the support of $x(\tau)$. This is the start of overlap, so it explains why $y(t)$ changes from zero to a nonzero piece after a.

At $t=b$, the endpoint alignment changes inside the nonzero region. In the sketch, the supports are aligned at their maximum overlap, so after b the overlap no longer grows in the same way. This creates a new piece of $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.latex: t=b:\quad \text{overlap changes from growing to shrinking}

explanation_blocks.text: At $t=c$, the shifted support of $h(t-\tau)$ reaches the last contact with the support of $x(\tau)$. After that time there is no overlap, so $y(t)$ returns to zero.
So the breakpoints are not arbitrary features of the formula. They come from support events in the convolution: overlap begins at a, the overlap pattern changes at b, and overlap ends at c.

sections.lesson_title: Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Explaining Output Shape from the Input and Impulse Response

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with three aligned time-domain plots using a shared horizontal time scale. Top plot: $x(t)$ as a wider finite-duration rectangular pulse. Middle plot: $h(t)$ as a shorter finite-duration rectangular pulse. Bottom plot: the computed output $y(t)$ as a trapezoidal finite-duration signal with breakpoints labeled a, b, c, and d. Label the $y(t)$ intervals as zero before a, rising on $a<t<b$, level on $b<t<c$, falling on $c<t<d$, and zero after d. Keep the figure uncluttered and do not include convolution calculations.

example_content.example_prompt: Plots of a finite-duration input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and computed output $y(t)$ are shown. Explain why $y(t)$ first rises, then levels off, and finally falls.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shape of the computed output $y(t)$. To explain that shape, connect each interval of $y(t)$ to how $x(\tau)$ overlaps the shifted impulse response $h(t-\tau)$ as t moves.
From the plot, the nonzero output is divided into three behavior intervals: $y(t)$ rises from a to b, stays level from b to c, and falls from c to d.

On the first interval, the shifted $h(t-\tau)$ is entering the support of $x(\tau)$. More of the two signals overlap as t increases, so the weighted overlap in the integral increases. That is why $y(t)$ rises.
On the middle interval, the shorter pulse is fully inside the longer pulse. The amount of overlap stays the same, so the convolution output stays level instead of continuing to rise.

explanation_blocks.latex: b<t<c:\quad \text{overlap stays constant}\Rightarrow y(t)\text{ levels off}

explanation_blocks.text: On the final nonzero interval, $h(t-\tau)$ is leaving the support of $x(\tau)$. The overlap shrinks as t increases, so the value of the integral decreases. That is why $y(t)$ falls back to zero.
So the output shape is not explained by $x(t)$ alone or $h(t)$ alone. It comes from their joint overlap inside the convolution integral.

sections.lesson_title: Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Summarizing the LTI System Response from the Piecewise Output

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional figure showing a final piecewise output $y(t)$ for an LTI system. Include a small block diagram $x(t)$ -> $h(t)$ -> $y(t)$ above the plot. The $y(t)$ plot should have a horizontal t-axis, visible zero regions before a and after d, and marked breakpoints a, b, c, and d. Label the nonzero regions as rising on $a<t<b$, level on $b<t<c$, and falling on $c<t<d$. Keep the visual focused on summarizing the output behavior; do not include convolution calculations or extra signal plots.

example_content.example_prompt: A computed piecewise output $y(t)$ is shown for an LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$. Summarize the system's time-domain output behavior.

explanation_blocks.text: The plotted piecewise function is the system output $y(t)$. Since the system is LTI, this output is the convolution of the given input $x(t)$ with the impulse response $h(t)$.
Start the summary by stating the support. The output is zero before the first breakpoint a, nonzero from a to d, and zero again after d.
Next, name the breakpoints that divide the response into time regions. Here, the relevant breakpoints are a, b, c, and d.
Now describe the behavior inside the nonzero interval. The output rises on the first nonzero interval, stays level in the middle interval, and falls on the final nonzero interval.

A concise response summary is: for this input and impulse response, the LTI system output is zero until a, turns on and rises from a to b, remains level from b to c, falls from c to d, and is zero after d.

The final phrase matters: this is the response to the given $x(t)$ through the system with impulse response $h(t)$, not a behavior of $x(t)$ alone, $h(t)$ alone, or the system independent of its input.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and the computed convolution shown below. Which statement correctly identifies the output $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the output equals the convolution of the input with the impulse response.
Since the computed convolution is $p(t)$, the output is $y(t)=p(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and the computed convolution shown below. Which statement correctly identifies the output $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the output is the convolution result. The convolution may be written as h*x or x*h.
Since the computed convolution is $r(t)$, the output is $y(t)=r(t)$.

Plot $y(t)=0 for t<-1$, a nonzero finite-duration triangular curve from $t=-1 to t=3$, and $y(t)=0 for t>3$. Label the breakpoints -1 and 3 on the t-axis. Create a clean black-and-white time-domain plot of the convolution output $y(t)$. Show a horizontal t-axis and a vertical $y(t)$-axis. Plot $y(t)=0 for t<2$, a nonzero finite-duration rounded hump from $t=2 to t=6$, and $y(t)=0 for t>6$. Label the breakpoints 2 and 6 on the t-axis. Make the zero line visible before 2 and after 6. Do not use open or closed endpoint styling.

prompt_blocks.text: The plot shows the convolution output $y(t)$. State where $y(t)$ is nonzero, and state where $y(t)=0$.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)$ is nonzero for $-1<t<3$, and $y(t)=0$ for $t<-1$ and $t>3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the plotted curve as $y(t)$. The output leaves the zero line at $t=-1$ and returns to the zero line at $t=3$.
The endpoint convention is not the focus here; -1 and 3 are the support boundaries.

prompt_blocks.text: The plot shows the convolution output $y(t)$. State where $y(t)$ is nonzero, and state where $y(t)=0$.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)$ is nonzero for $2<t<6$, and $y(t)=0$ for $t<2$ and $t>6$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the plotted curve as $y(t)$. The output leaves the zero line at $t=2$ and returns to the zero line at $t=6$.
The endpoint convention is not the focus here; 2 and 6 are the support boundaries.

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with four aligned panels. Panel 1: a fixed rectangular support for $x(\tau)$ on a $\tau$-axis from $\tau=0 to \tau=4$. Panels 2-4: matching $\tau$-axes showing the shifted support of $h(t-\tau)$ at $t=p$, $t=q$, and $t=r$, with overlap against $x(\tau)$ highlighted. At $t=p$, the right endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the left endpoint of $x(\tau)$, so overlap begins. At $t=q$, the supports are exactly aligned with maximum overlap; highlight this panel. At $t=r$, the left endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the right endpoint of $x(\tau)$, so overlap ends. Add a small $y(t)$ plot at the bottom with breakpoints p, q, and r marked, and visually emphasize the breakpoint q.

Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with four aligned panels. Panel 1: a fixed rectangular support for $x(\tau)$ on a $\tau$-axis from $\tau=-2 to \tau=3$. Panels 2-4: matching $\tau$-axes showing the shifted support of $h(t-\tau)$ at $t=a$, $t=b$, and $t=c$, with overlap against $x(\tau)$ highlighted. At $t=a$, the right endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the left endpoint of $x(\tau)$, so overlap begins. At $t=b$, the supports have a marked endpoint alignment inside the nonzero region and the overlap pattern changes while overlap remains nonzero. At $t=c$, the left endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the right endpoint of $x(\tau)$, so overlap ends; highlight this panel. Add a small $y(t)$ plot at the bottom with breakpoints a, b, and c marked, and visually emphasize the breakpoint c.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a piecewise convolution output with breakpoints $p<q<r$. Which overlap change explains the breakpoint at $t=q$?

choice_blocks.text: The shifted support first touches the support of $x(\tau)$, so overlap begins.
The supports reach maximum alignment, so the overlap changes from growing to shrinking.
The shifted support has moved completely past $x(\tau)$, so overlap ends.
Only the height of $h(t-\tau)$ changes; the support overlap stays the same.
The supports still partially overlap, but the output should be treated as zero.

questions.correct_answer: The supports reach maximum alignment at $t=q$, so the overlap changes from growing to shrinking.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A breakpoint marks a support event in the convolution overlap. At $t=q$, the supports are aligned at maximum overlap, so after q the overlap no longer grows in the same way.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: t=q:\quad \text{overlap changes from growing to shrinking}

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a piecewise convolution output with breakpoints $a<b<c$. Which overlap change explains the breakpoint at $t=c$?

choice_blocks.text: The shifted support first touches $x(\tau)$, so overlap begins.
The supports reach an interior alignment, so overlap changes pattern while remaining nonzero.
The shifted support reaches its last contact with $x(\tau)$, so after this time no overlap remains.
Only the amplitude of $x(\tau)$ changes; no support endpoint event occurs.
The overlap is increasing at $t=c$, so the output has just turned on.

questions.correct_answer: At $t=c$, the shifted support reaches its last contact with $x(\tau)$, so the overlap ends.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At the last breakpoint, the moving support has reached its final contact with the fixed support. After that point, the two supports no longer overlap, so the output returns to zero.

sections.section_title: Explaining Output Shape from the Input and Impulse Response

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with three aligned time-domain plots using a shared horizontal time scale. Top plot: $x(t)$ as a wider finite-duration rectangular pulse from $t=0 to t=6$. Middle plot: $h(t)$ as a shorter finite-duration rectangular pulse from $t=0 to t=2$. Bottom plot: the computed output $y(t)$ as a trapezoidal finite-duration signal with breakpoints labeled a, b, c, and d. Label the $y(t)$ intervals as zero before a, rising on $a<t<b$, level on $b<t<c$, falling on $c<t<d$, and zero after d. Keep the figure uncluttered and do not include convolution calculations.

Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with three aligned time-domain plots using a shared horizontal time scale. Top plot: $x(t)$ as a finite-duration triangular pulse that rises linearly to a peak and then falls linearly back to zero. Middle plot: $h(t)$ as a short finite-duration rectangular pulse. Bottom plot: the computed output $y(t)$ as a single smooth finite-duration hump with breakpoints labeled a, b, and c. Label the $y(t)$ intervals as zero before a, rising on $a<t<b$, falling on $b<t<c$, and zero after c. Do not show a plateau. Keep the figure uncluttered and do not include convolution calculations.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the plots of $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and the resulting $y(t)$, which explanation best accounts for why $y(t)$ rises, levels off, and then falls?

choice_blocks.text: The output has that shape because $x(t)$ is wide; $h(t)$ does not affect the rise, level part, or fall.
The overlap between $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ increases, then stays constant while the shorter pulse is fully inside the longer one, then decreases.
The output has that shape because $h(t)$ is short; $x(t)$ only sets the final endpoint.
The overlap first decreases, then stays constant, then increases, so $y(t)$ falls, levels off, and rises.
The plateau appears because endpoints are labeled b and c, even though the amount of overlap is still changing there.

questions.correct_answer: The output rises as overlap increases, stays level while the overlap amount is constant, and falls as overlap decreases.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shape of $y(t)$ comes from the joint overlap in the convolution integral, not from either signal alone. More overlap gives the rising segment, constant full overlap gives the level segment, and shrinking overlap gives the falling segment.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: a<t<b:\ \text{overlap increases},\quad b<t<c:\ \text{overlap is constant},\quad c<t<d:\ \text{overlap decreases}

prompt_blocks.text: Given the plots of $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and the resulting $y(t)$, which explanation best accounts for why $y(t)$ rises to a peak and then falls?

choice_blocks.text: The output follows the triangular input $x(t)$ alone; $h(t)$ only changes the height scale.
Because $h(t)$ is rectangular, $y(t)$ must stay level throughout the entire nonzero interval.
The overlap decreases first and then increases, so the output falls before it rises.
As $h(t-\tau)$ overlaps larger values of $x(\tau)$, the weighted overlap grows; after it moves past the largest part of $x(\tau)$, the weighted overlap shrinks.
The labels a, b, and c explain the shape by themselves; the amount or weight of overlap does not matter.

questions.correct_answer: The output rises while the weighted overlap with larger values of $x(\tau)$ grows, then falls after that weighted overlap shrinks.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: With a triangular input, the output shape depends on weighted overlap, not just the presence of any overlap. The value of $y(t)$ grows while the shifted impulse response overlaps larger portions of $x(\tau)$, then decreases after the overlap shifts away from the peak.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: a<t<b:\ \text{weighted overlap increases},\qquad b<t<c:\ \text{weighted overlap decreases}

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional figure showing a final piecewise output $y(t)$ for an LTI system. Include a small block diagram $x(t)$ -> $h(t)$ -> $y(t)$ above the plot. The $y(t)$ plot should have a horizontal t-axis, visible zero regions before p and after s, and marked breakpoints p, q, r, and s. Label the nonzero regions as rising on $p<t<q$, level on $q<t<r$, and falling on $r<t<s$. Keep the visual focused on summarizing the output behavior; do not include convolution calculations or extra signal plots.

Create a clean black-and-white instructional figure showing a final piecewise output $y(t)$ for an LTI system. Include a small block diagram $x(t)$ -> $h(t)$ -> $y(t)$ above the plot. The $y(t)$ plot should have a horizontal t-axis, visible zero regions before a and after c, and marked breakpoints a, b, and c. Label the nonzero regions as rising on $a<t<b and falling on b<t<c$. Do not show a level interval. Keep the visual focused on summarizing the output behavior; do not include convolution calculations or extra signal plots.

prompt_blocks.text: A piecewise convolution output $y(t)$ for an LTI system is shown. Which summary correctly describes the system output?

choice_blocks.text: For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before p and after s, nonzero on $p<t<s$, rises on $p<t<q$, stays level on $q<t<r$, and falls on $r<t<s$.
For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before p and nonzero after p; the graph only shows where the response starts.
For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ rises on $p<t<q$, falls on $q<t<r$, and stays level on $r<t<s$.
The plot summarizes $h(t)$: the impulse response rises, stays level, and falls between p and s.
The LTI system will always have this same output shape for any input because the breakpoints are system properties.

questions.correct_answer: For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before p and after s, nonzero on $p<t<s$, rises on $p<t<q$, stays level on $q<t<r$, and falls on $r<t<s$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A complete output summary names the zero regions, the nonzero support, the breakpoints, and the behavior inside each nonzero interval. It must also describe the response for the given input and impulse response, not $h(t)$ alone or a system property independent of input.

prompt_blocks.text: A piecewise convolution output $y(t)$ for an LTI system is shown. Which summary correctly describes the system output?

choice_blocks.text: For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is nonzero before a, rises on $a<t<b$, falls on $b<t<c$, and is zero after c.
For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before a and after c, nonzero on $a<t<c$, rises on $a<t<b$, and falls on $b<t<c$.
For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before a and after c, but it falls on $a<t<b$ and rises on $b<t<c$.
The plot summarizes the input $x(t)$: the input turns on at a, peaks at b, and turns off at c.
The system itself rises from a to b and falls from b to c no matter what input is applied.

questions.correct_answer: For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before a and after c, nonzero on $a<t<c$, rises on $a<t<b$, and falls on $b<t<c$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The plotted piecewise function is the output $y(t)$. The correct summary includes both zero regions, the full nonzero interval, and the rise-then-fall behavior for the response to the given input through the LTI system.

image_records.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with four aligned panels. Panel 1: a fixed rectangular support for $x(\tau)$ on a $\tau$-axis from $\tau=0 to \tau=4$. Panels 2-4: matching $\tau$-axes showing the shifted support of $h(t-\tau)$ at $t=p$, $t=q$, and $t=r$, with overlap against $x(\tau)$ highlighted. At $t=p$, the right endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the left endpoint of $x(\tau)$, so overlap begins. At $t=q$, the supports are exactly aligned with maximum overlap; highlight this panel. At $t=r$, the left endpoint of $h(t-\tau)$ just touches the right endpoint of $x(\tau)$, so overlap ends. Add a small $y(t)$ plot at the bottom with breakpoints p, q, and r marked, and visually emphasize the breakpoint q.
